cards.back: Observable artifact of a compromise: malware hash, C2 IP address, domain, registry key. Static, easy to block, quickly outdated.
Characteristic behavior of an attack: encoded PowerShell, anomalous outbound connection, sudden privilege escalation. More durable than an IOC, harder to detect.
Two authentications too far apart in time and space for physical travel. Suggests credential or session theft; check VPN and proxy before concluding.
The same account active from two locations at the same time. Distinct from impossible travel: here sessions are concurrent, suggesting sharing or token theft.
Clearing, truncating, or disabling auditing by an attacker to destroy evidence. Serious signal: Windows Event ID 1102 (security log cleared).
Encrypts data and demands payment. Indicators: changed file extensions, ransom notes, mass file access, deletion of shadow copies.
A worm self-propagates over the network without user action. A virus requires a host (file, boot sector) and execution.
Disguises itself as legitimate software to be executed. It does not self-propagate or infect other files: it opens a backdoor.
Hides compromise at the kernel or firmware level. Indicators: discrepancies between tools, hidden processes, persistence after reinstallation.
Lives in memory with no file on disk. Relies on native tools (PowerShell, WMI, mshta, regsvr32): "living off the land." EDR and behavioral telemetry are required.
Code that triggers an action on a specific date or event. Indicators: conditional code, suspicious scheduled task, trigger account or file.
Spyware collects information (browsing, keystrokes, screen). Adware displays ads, often bundled with free software. Both can exfiltrate data.
Attacker intercepts between two parties to read, modify, or replay traffic. Without encryption they see everything; with properly validated TLS they only see ciphertext.
Forces negotiation down to a weak version (TLS 1.0/1.1). Indicators: handshake alerts, abnormally low negotiated version.
Cache poisoning or DNS tunneling. Indicators: inconsistent responses, large TXT queries, resolution to an unexpected IP.
Unauthorized equipment on the network: rogue access point, switch, unauthorized DHCP. Indicators: new MAC address, active port, unknown DHCP lease.
Tailgating: following an authorized person without badging (countermeasure: mantrap). Shoulder surfing: reading over someone's shoulder (countermeasure: privacy screen, positioning).
Phishing = mass email. Spear = targeted at a person or department. Whaling = targets an executive (wire transfer, confidential attachment).
Vishing = phone. Smishing = SMS. Quishing = QR code. The channel changes, the principle remains: obtain credentials, payment, or execution.
AI-generated video or voice used for BEC/CEO fraud or extortion. Defense: out-of-band verification, payment approval procedure.
Attacker compromises a legitimate site frequented by the target to infect its visitors. Indicator is a change in behavior of a trusted site.
Unvalidated input is interpreted as code. Principle: mixing data and instructions. Structural defense: parameterized queries, strict validation, least privilege.
Brute force: many attempts on one account. Password spraying: one common password across many accounts, to avoid per-account lockout.
Accessing a file outside the intended directory via ../ or %2e%2e. Indicator: requests containing these sequences; defense: canonicalization and allowlisting.
